# Figma MCP + Code Connect: The Complete Guide to AI-Powered Design-to-Code Workflows

[![Mageswari](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*O91TqjOu7ehPwvLLj88wUA.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@Rythmuxdesigner?source=post_page---byline--5c759a6027f8---------------------------------------)

The design-to-code workflow has been broken for decades. Designers create pixel-perfect interfaces. Developers manually translate those designs into code. Somewhere between Figma and GitHub, the magic slips away spacing drifts by 2px, colors shift slightly, components get rebuilt from scratch instead of reused. It’s nobody’s fault, just a broken workflow that has resisted every attempt at automation.

That changed in 2026. Figma’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, combined with Code Connect, has created something unprecedented: a direct neural link between design files and code repositories. AI agents can now read Figma designs with semantic understanding, generate code using your actual components, and even push working UI back to Figma for visual refinement .

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*9WaL55i_M_FOqewvU3GCdg.jpeg)

This isn’t another design-to-code export tool. It’s a fundamental shift in how design and engineering collaborate. Here’s the complete guide to understanding, implementing, and mastering this workflow.

## What Is Figma MCP: The Technical Foundation

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard created by Anthropic that allows AI agents to interact with external data sources through a standardized interface . Think of it as a “USB-C port for AI applications” a universal connector that lets any AI tool plug into any data source.

Figma’s MCP server applies this protocol specifically to design files. Instead of AI tools guessing design intent from screenshots or static images, they access structured design data directly: component hierarchies, design tokens, Auto Layout constraints, and Code Connect mappings .

The architecture has three components:

1. MCP Host: Your coding environment (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex)
2. MCP Client: Maintains the connection between host and server
3. MCP Server: Interfaces with Figma, exposing design data as structured context

When you reference a Figma node, the server returns not just visual information, but semantic understanding: this is a Button component using the primary variant, with 16px padding, using the color token `action-primary`…

# I Gave My Agent CLAUDE.md and DESIGN.md. It Ignored My Entire Component Library.

## Why AI coding agents need more than design tokens to understand your actual component system

[![Surendar Selvaraj](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*3uxTzP6B2AoY2yPssn9DBw.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@surendarselvaraj?source=post_page---byline--c6d7e9be34d4---------------------------------------)

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*Kum1YD2Uyco_wLEeRbwgvQ.jpeg)

### There is a moment every designer hits when they start working with coding agents.

You have done everything right. You have a CLAUDE.md telling the agent how to behave. You have a DESIGN.md with every token, every color, every spacing value. You run the agent. It generates a screen.

And somewhere in that screen is a button it built from scratch.

Not your button. Its button. Using your colors, your border radius, your spacing tokens. But not your component. Never your component.

That was the moment I realised the stack was incomplete.

## What Each File Actually Does

By now most people working with agents know the pattern.

CLAUDE.md is the behaviour file. It tells the agent how to work. What rules to follow. What to never do. How to name files, structure code, handle edge cases. It was popularised by the Claude Code workflow and spread fast because it works. It keeps agents consistent across sessions.

DESIGN.md is an emerging documentation pattern inspired by recent agent-first workflows and open design token standards. It is a single file with 2 parts: YAML front matter containing your machine-readable tokens, and markdown prose explaining the why behind every decision. Color values with semantic meaning. Typography with rationale. Spacing with intent. It is the file your design system was always missing for agents.

Together they cover a lot.

CLAUDE.md: how the agent behaves. DESIGN.md: what the tokens are and why they exist.

But here is what neither file covers.

What your components are. When to use them. When not to. Which one to reach for when 3 of them could technically work. What states every component must handle before it ships.

That gap is where agents break down. Quietly, confidently, and at scale.

## Why Tokens Are Not Enough

When I first set up DESIGN.md for our system, I assumed the token coverage would solve most problems. The agent would see `color.brand.primary` with its semantic label and use it correctly. It would read the spacing scale and apply the right value. It would stop improvising.

It did stop improvising on tokens. I will give it that.

But components were a different story entirely.

Our Figma library had 60+ components. The agent knew none of them existed. It could not open Figma mid-session. It had no reference pointing to the library. So it did what any reasonable system does when given no constraints: it built what it needed from available materials.

It saw our tokens. It built components. They looked right. They were wrong.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*wr5MA9BqXEaIjTuMWTNEwA.png)

A card with a hardcoded action div instead of ButtonPrimary. An input with a raw HTML element instead of FormField. A notification banner rebuilt from scratch instead of using AlertBanner.

Every one of those was a missing sentence in our documentation. A component that existed but was never introduced to the agent.

## The Missing File

CLAUDE.md handles behaviour. DESIGN.md handles tokens. What we needed was a third file handling components.

We called it `system.md`.

Not a replacement for your full documentation. Not another Zeroheight page nobody reads. A dense, agent-optimised file that lives in your repo and answers 3 questions for every component:

1. What is this?
2. When do you use it?
3. When do you not?

For our ButtonPrimary it looked like this:

```
ButtonPrimary
Use: single primary action per view
Do not use: inside cards, modals, or repeated in a list
Never: place 2 ButtonPrimary components in the same section
```

3 lines. That is enough. The agent stops guessing and starts following.

We did the same for every component in the library. The whole file took one afternoon. The difference in agent output was immediate.

## One Example, Start to Finish

Token: `color.neutral.subtle`

DESIGN.md entry: background surface color, non-interactive use.

What the agent did anyway: used it as body text color on a dark card. The contrast ratio failed WCAG. The text was barely readable.

We could have fixed the prompt. Added “do not use subtle tokens on text.” But that just moves the assumption from the file into the prompt. Next session, gone.

So we added one line to `system.md` instead:

```
color.neutral.subtle
Use for: non-interactive background surfaces only
Do not use for: text, borders, icons, or interactive elements
```

Next session. Correct output. No prompt change needed.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*xATVXNL9A3HDWqvH9NmJMA.png)

That is the pattern. Every time the agent gets something wrong, the fix is almost never the prompt. It is a missing sentence that a human never needed because they already knew. The agent does not know. Write it down.

## Where to Fix It in Figma First

Before `system.md` can be accurate, the source has to be right. That means 3 layers in Figma.

## Get Surendar Selvaraj’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe

Subscribe

Remember me for faster sign in

**Layer 1: Variables description field**

Every Figma variable has a description field. Almost nobody fills it in.

Open your variable collection. Find `color.neutral.subtle`. Add:

```
Use for non-interactive background surfaces only.
Not for text, borders, icons, or interactive elements.
```

When you export tokens through Tokens Studio or Style Dictionary, that description travels with the value. The agent reads it. The rule lands without you repeating it in every session.

**Layer 2: Dev Mode component notes**

Figma’s Dev Mode lets you add notes directly to components. Answer 3 questions per component:

1. What is this?
2. When do you use it?
3. When do you not?

For CardWithCTA:

```
Use when the card requires exactly one primary action.
Do not use for dashboard widgets or read-only content cards.
Always pair with ButtonPrimary only. Never a text link.
```

Write for zero context. Pretend the reader has never seen your system. Because the agent hasn’t.

**Layer 3: system.md in your repo**

Figma lives inside Figma. The agent working in your codebase cannot open it mid-session.

`system.md` is the bridge. It pulls everything into one flat file the agent can read from the repo directly. Token rules from your variables. Component rules from your Dev Mode notes. Global rules that apply across everything.

Paste it at the start of every agent session. Or reference it in CLAUDE.md so the agent always loads it automatically.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*nb73VcBxeD57-iL02dfcPQ.png)

## The Full Stack

Here is how the 3 files divide the work:

**CLAUDE.md:** How the agent behaves. Coding standards, naming rules, file structure, what to never do.

**DESIGN.md:** What the tokens are and why. Colors with semantic roles. Typography with rationale. Spacing with intent. A structured, agent-readable format that works well across Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot workflows.

You can find the full spec and fork it at [https://github.com/google/design-md](https://github.com/google/design-md).

**system.md:** What your components are and how to use them. When to reach for ButtonPrimary vs ButtonGhost. What FormField wraps. What states every component must handle before it ships.

3 files. Each doing a job the others cannot.

The moment I stopped trying to fix everything through prompts and started maintaining these 3 files properly, agent output changed. Not slightly. Noticeably. Components from the library. Tokens used correctly. Spacing consistent. States handled.

Not because the agent got smarter. Because the documentation finally got honest.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*pqONfcKbT4mJ8gfB6Ckw0A.png)

## What This Actually Revealed

The uncomfortable part of this process was not the extra files. It was what filling them in exposed.

For every component we documented in `system.md`, there was a rule we had been applying unconsciously for years. CardWithCTA is not for dashboard widgets. We all knew that. Nobody had written it. We never needed to because everyone on the team already knew.

The agent did not know. And writing it down for the agent meant writing it down properly for the first time.

I remember looking at the completed `system.md` after a few weeks and realising we had finally surfaced 3 years of institutional memory. Rules that lived in Slack threads, onboarding calls, and the heads of the 2 designers who had been there from the start.

The agent did not break our design system. It just stopped pretending it was complete.

Do not try to document everything at once. Pick one surface. One set of components. One page type.

Fill in the Figma variable descriptions for every token on that surface. Add Dev Mode notes to every component it uses. Write the `system.md` entries for those components only.

Run the agent. See what breaks. Fix the file, not the prompt. Prompts disappear after the session. System knowledge compounds.

That loop is faster than it sounds. And each round makes `system.md` more useful for the agent and more honest for the next designer who joins your team.

I built a `system.md` template on GitHub with the full structure: tokens, components, global rules, and a state checklist. Fork it, replace the placeholders with your own system, and you have a working starting point in under an hour.

[**Checkout GitHub Link**](https://github.com/designbysuren/ds-manifest) **\|** [**Checkout Figma Community file**](https://www.figma.com/community/file/1638386195517568464/system-md-agent-ready-design-system-template)

CLAUDE.md told the agent how to code. DESIGN.md told it what the tokens mean. `system.md` told it what we actually built.

All 3 together is the first time our design system was fully legible to something that could not guess.

We spent 3 years building a system for designers. It took an agent that cannot guess to finally make us build one for real.
